item.content:encoded:
I know I'm a few years late to this, but I really don't like the Xyank additions.
Without them, this is a cool article about Clark's Third Law in action, and things like that.
With them, it's the story of a bunch of idiots who have a time traveller on their payroll, but choose to ignore him.
The edits change the tone and focus of the article, and because they're right at the end that's what you're leaving with.

In general I just don't think that this needs to be linked to the Temporal Anomalies Department, and that doing so ruins them. In a canon where the TAD exists, this time traveller wouldn't be an anomaly like this.

item.title: Staff Post - Open
item.content:encoded:
Timer Expired. Edits made as discussed below. Author may revert at any time.

The WikiWalk team is proposing edits to this page. All proposed edits will be in a collapsible below this post, and after 7 days if there are no serious objections to the edits, the feedback received will be taken into account as the edits are made. If you have questions not directly related to the article about this project, please pm a member of the WikiWalk Team

+ Show Block
- Hide Block

Yes. Not even the EX articles are safe from the Grand Crosslinking. Considering how this article can essentially boil down to the SCPF acquiring a genuine time traveler and then letting them age to death, you'd think someone in the Temporal Anomalies department might have words about such a fantastic waste of resources. As such, I'm recommending the addition of a few short addenda:

Adding the following before addenda after the list of events predicted by 711-EX:

Addendum 711-2: Dr. Xyank of the Temporal Anomalies Department has made multiple requests to return SCP-711 back to the point in time from which it claims to have been displaced. All requests have been denied.

We don't need to contain this person for no reason. He's verified. Let me take him home. ~ Dr. Xyank

And adding the following to the end of the piece:

I hope you're all very proud of yourselves. ~ Dr. Xyank

In this way, Dr. Xyank highlights just how poorly managed this anomaly is, again considering how it is a time traveler that the Foundation just contains until dead. Normally I wouldn't be so invasive with a WikiWalk proposal, but such a link not only hooks this EX up to the Foundation's temporal anomalies department, but all the other temporal anomalies that the Xyank tale series hooks up to in turn. Thats a lot of WikiWalk potential there.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

I used to have one of these - in 2007/8. CRAPPY display, but matches the specs.

Forty years? A full century? All we know is the word "Negro" was still in common use. Plus, did he age? Did he age normally? What did he OF?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Actually… They've had diodes for a long time, and could make them emit light, so it's not a stretch that's how they'd be described. The practical use of the LCD came MUCH later.

LCDs don't bear much resemblance to LEDs, and the science of liquid crystals wouldn't have been novel - if the dude said "that's a liquid crystal display," SCP researchers would reasonably be able to verify that. Even if he didn't, dismantling it would still yield polarized layers, a backlight, and a flexible sheet with goo in it - nothing at all like early LED prototypes.

Depends what type of phone it is. Early camera-phones didn't have THAT great a display.

He's from 2008 or later. The phone's a slider with a full keyboard. This ain't some ancient Nokia.

Actually… They've had diodes for a long time, and could make them emit light, so it's not a stretch that's how they'd be described. The practical use of the LCD came MUCH later.

shouldn't that be several hundred thousand?

Why is this ("rechargeable") being phrased with such skepticism?

Car batteries have been rechargeable for the longest time, and the entire structure of the inside of the phone would point to "Hey, you stick something in this end with power and it recharges!" They would actually be more shocked by the concept that it was a radio capable of transmission and reception simultaneously while still being incredibley tiny - and that they would be so cheap a kid would have one!
